reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: a request-success SLO of 99.9% over 28 days, with 20,000,000 valid requests expected in the window. The migration will route 10,000,000 of those requests through a new path that is estimated, before any test, to fail 0.05% of them. All figures are invented.

Derivation: the window's budget is 0.001 × 20,000,000 = 20,000 failed requests. At 70% used, 14,000 are spent and 6,000 remain. The migration's expected cost is 0.0005 × 10,000,000 = 5,000 failures, which would leave 1,000, or 5% of the budget, for the rest of the window.

Independent check: if the failure estimate is off by a factor of two, the migration costs 10,000 failures, 4,000 more than the remaining 6,000, so the budget would be exhausted and the SLO missed. The decision depends on how much the estimate can be trusted.

Misconception to reject: 'the expected cost fits, so proceed in one step.' A plan that consumes 83% of the remaining budget (5,000 / 6,000) on an untested estimate leaves almost no margin for anything else that goes wrong in the window.

Change one factor: start with a canary of 1% of the migration traffic (100,000 requests). At the estimated rate it costs 0.0005 × 100,000 = 50 failures and measures the real failure rate before most of the budget is committed.

Source and limits: error budgets and their use in release decisions are described in chapter 3 of Google's Site Reliability Engineering book, https://sre.google/sre-book/embracing-risk/, and in chapter 2 of The Site Reliability Workbook, https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/. reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: the load balancer logs in UTC, the application logs in Pacific Standard Time (UTC−8), and the paging system's clock is 2 minutes slow. All events are invented. The lab's first rule is to convert every timestamp to one reference before computing any interval.

Derivation: the load balancer shows errors rising at 14:03 UTC; the application log's first error at 06:03 PST is the same moment (14:03 UTC). The alert fired at 14:11 UTC. Independent check: from the normalized times, the detection delay is 14:11 − 14:03 = 8 minutes, the time to acknowledge is 5 minutes, the time to mitigate from the alert is 41 minutes, user impact until mitigation lasted 49 minutes, and the time to resolve from the alert is 89 minutes. The segments 8 + 41 = 49 minutes agree with the impact duration.

Misconception to reject: 'use the timestamps as logged.' Taking the pager's 14:14 at face value gives a 3-minute acknowledgement instead of 5, and mixing PST and UTC would make the application errors appear eight hours before the incident.

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: in a 40-hour (2,400-minute) week an engineer renews certificates by hand 15 times at 24 minutes each, restarts a stuck batch job 20 times at 18 minutes, grants access requests 60 times at 6 minutes and triages routine tickets 12 times at 20 minutes. Derivation: the four repeating tasks take 360 + 360 + 360 + 240 = 1,320 minutes, which is 1,320 / 2,400 = 55% of the week. They are manual, repetitive, automatable and without enduring value, so they meet the SRE book's description of toil; design reviews and project work do not.
Independent check: 1,320 + 300 + 780 = 2,400 minutes, so the inventory accounts for the whole week, and toil exceeds the book's goal of keeping operational work below 50% of an engineer's time.
Misconception to reject: 'any operational task is toil.' Work with enduring value, such as a design review that prevents a class of failures, is not toil even when it is not project work.

Change one factor: automate certificate renewal at a one-time cost of 16 hours (960 minutes). Toil falls to 960 minutes, 40% of the week, and the automation pays for itself after 960 / 360 ≈ 2.7 weeks.

Source and limits: chapter 5 of Google's Site Reliability Engineering book, 'Eliminating Toil', defines toil as manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical work without enduring value that scales linearly as a service grows, and states a goal of keeping it below 50% of each SRE's time: https://sre.google/sre-book/eliminating-toil/.
